title: Evaluate an AI model's quality before launch
summary: AI features can give different answers to the same question and can be confidently wrong. Before launch, define what 'good enough' means and test the AI against a set of realistic examples, then keep testing after release.

beginner: Write down what the AI feature must do well, in measurable terms. For example: 'answers are accurate for at least 95% of common questions', 'never gives personal advice', 'replies within 3 seconds'.
Collect a test set: 30 to 50 realistic examples to start, taken from real user questions where you are allowed to use them. Include easy cases, hard cases, edge cases and attempts to misuse it.
For each example, write what a good answer looks like, or the rules a good answer must follow.
Run the test set and score the results. Simple checks can be automated; others need a person, or another AI model, to grade against clear rules. Check a sample of any AI grading by hand.
Check for harm and fairness: does it treat different user groups equally, does it make things up, and does it refuse when it should? Involve your legal or data protection colleagues.
Agree a launch decision with the team based on the scores. Keep the test set and rerun it whenever the model, prompt or data changes, and keep monitoring after launch.
intermediate: Define specific, measurable success criteria across accuracy, safety, tone, speed and cost.
Build a test set of realistic, edge and adversarial cases with expected outcomes.
Grade with a mix of code checks, model grading and human review, and validate the model grading by hand.
Make a launch decision against thresholds, and rerun the evaluation as a regression check on every change.
experienced: Agree multi-dimensional success criteria with thresholds.
Build a representative test set, including edge, misuse and fairness cases.
Validate the grading approach and make results reproducible.
Run the evaluation on every model or prompt change, and monitor live for drift and hallucination.

canDelegateTo.task: Build and run the evaluation and grading
Write edge cases and misuse cases for the test set
Review for data protection, fairness and harm risks
Test the AI feature with real users and capture where it confuses them

toolExamples.claude: Ask Claude to help draft success criteria and edge cases for your feature, then review every one yourself. Anthropic's docs on defining success criteria and building evaluations give a worked approach.
toolExamples.github: Keep the test set and expected answers in the repository, so the evaluation can run automatically when the prompt or model changes.
toolExamples.confluence: Keep an evaluation page with the success criteria, thresholds, the latest scores and the launch decision.
toolExamples.jira: Raise each failing example as a bug linked to the AI feature, so fixes can be retested against the same case.

definitionOfDone: Measurable success criteria and thresholds agreed
Test set covers normal, edge and misuse cases
Results scored, with any AI grading checked by a person
Launch decision recorded, and evaluation set to rerun on every change
pitfalls: Testing with a handful of hand-picked examples
Trusting AI-graded scores without checking them
Evaluating once before launch and never again

leaderView.good: AI quality is measured against agreed tests before launch.
ask: What does good enough look like, and how did we measure it?
How does the model do on difficult or sensitive cases?
signs: Quality is judged by a few demos.
There's no agreed bar for launch.
